title: Sticks for Digits
question: On a seven-segment display, digits are drawn with straight segments. How many segments are needed to display the number 1234?
correctExplanation: Right. Two for the one, five for the two, five for the three, and four for the four total sixteen.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 16. Each digit has its own fixed segment count, so the totals simply add: two plus five plus five plus four. Treating digits as uniform is the trap.
lessonContent:
Bodies built from fixed parts allow exact counting.
Break compound objects into known components.
Different symbols can cost different amounts.
Summing parts beats estimating wholes.

title: Sticks for Thousand
question: Using seven-segment digits, how many segments are required to display the number 1000?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The one takes two segments and each zero takes six, giving two plus eighteen.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 20. The zeros dominate the cost because each requires a full loop of six segments. Multiplying the per-digit cost by the count is the efficient route.
lessonContent:
Repetition lets multiplication replace addition.
Spot the dominant component in a total.
Uniform parts scale predictably.
Quick multiplication beats careful counting.

title: Sticks for Eights
question: How many segments does a seven-segment display use to show four eights in a row?
correctExplanation: Right. Each eight uses all seven segments, and four of them total twenty-eight.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 28. The eight is the most expensive digit because it lights every segment. Multiplying seven by four gives the total once that maximum is recognised.
lessonContent:
Extremes define the boundaries of a system.
Knowing the maximum cost per unit speeds estimates.
Counting is fastest when multiplied by repetition.
Recognise which symbol is fully deployed.

title: One Painted Face
question: A large cube is painted on every face, then cut into twenty-seven equal small cubes. How many small cubes have exactly one painted face?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The centre cube of each of the six faces carries a single painted square.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Only the middle of each face keeps paint on one side, because edge and corner pieces catch more than one face. Visualising the grid position by position is the reliable method.
lessonContent:
Position in a structure determines its properties.
Corners, edges, and centres behave differently.
Classify by location before counting.
Three-dimensional grids reward careful visualisation.

title: Two Painted Faces
question: In that same painted cube cut into twenty-seven, how many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
correctExplanation: Right. Each of the twelve edges of the large cube holds exactly one middle piece with two painted faces.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. The middle cube of every edge touches exactly two faces, so the count equals the number of edges. Edges are the category to count, not faces.
lessonContent:
Match structural categories to their counts.
Edges form a natural home for two-face pieces.
Naming the location simplifies the arithmetic.
Geometry rewards vocabulary about parts.

title: Three Painted Faces
question: A painted three-by-three-by-three cube is taken apart. Counting only the pieces that sit at the vertices, how many are painted on three sides?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The eight corners each touch three faces and so carry three painted squares.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. Corners are where three faces meet, so each corner piece is painted on three sides. Counting vertices gives the answer directly.
lessonContent:
Vertices are where multiple surfaces intersect.
Each intersection multiplies the number of exposed areas.
Structural counts often equal corners or edges.
Recognising categories prevents recounting.

title: Bare Interior
question: In the same painted cube cut into twenty-seven, how many small cubes have no paint at all?
correctExplanation: Right. Only the single cube at the very centre is hidden from every face.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Interior pieces have no exposed surface, and a three-by-three-by-three arrangement leaves exactly one such position. Checking that the categories sum to twenty-seven confirms it.
lessonContent:
Interior regions are shielded from the outside.
Verify by adding all categories to the total.
Hidden positions have their own properties.
Complete accounting catches errors.

title: Four Cubed Paint
question: A cube made of sixty-four small cubes is painted all over. How many of the small cubes end up with no paint?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Stripping one layer from every side leaves a two-by-two-by-two interior of eight cubes.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. The unpainted core shrinks by one on each side in every direction, so a four-cube width becomes two. Cubing the reduced width gives eight.
lessonContent:
Interiors shrink by one layer per dimension.
Reduce each dimension before multiplying.
Powers model repeated shrinking neatly.
Generalise one case to check another.

title: Edges of a Cube
question: How many straight edges does a cube have?
correctExplanation: Right. Each of the six faces has four sides, and shared edges are counted one time each.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. Counting face sides directly double-counts because every edge belongs to two faces. Grouping the twelve segments by direction — four in each of three directions — is the cleanest check.
lessonContent:
Shared features need careful accounting to avoid double counting.
Grouping by direction reveals symmetry.
Simple shapes still hide counting subtleties.
Cross-check totals two different ways.

title: Meeting at a Corner
question: How many faces of a cube meet at a single corner?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Three mutually perpendicular faces meet at every vertex of a cube.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Each corner is an intersection of three surfaces, which is why corner pieces touch three sides. Visualising the meeting point beats memorising the number.
lessonContent:
Intersections define how many surfaces meet.
Mutually perpendicular surfaces create distinct corners.
Counting at a point is easier than counting globally.
Local inspection often settles global questions.

title: Unfolded Squares
question: How many square faces does the flat pattern of a cube contain?
correctExplanation: Right. Unfolding cannot create or destroy faces, so the pattern holds one square per side.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. A net is the same surface rearranged, so the count is preserved exactly. Unfolding changes arrangement, never quantity.
lessonContent:
Transformations can preserve counts while changing arrangement.
Nets are rearrangements, not new objects.
Conservation ideas appear in geometry too.
Check invariants when shapes move.

title: Punched and Folded
question: A sheet is folded in half five times, then a single hole is punched straight through the stack. When unfolded, how many holes appear?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Each fold doubles the layers, so five folds produce thirty-two layers and thirty-two holes.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 32. Doubling repeats five times, giving two to the fifth power. Counting layers rather than imagining unfolding is the reliable shortcut.
lessonContent:
Folding doubles the layer count each time.
Repeated doubling is exponentiation.
Counting layers predicts the unfolded result.
many small operations compound surprisingly fast.

title: Layers of Paper
question: How many layers thick is a sheet of paper after being folded in half three times?
correctExplanation: Right. Each fold doubles the stack, so three folds multiply one layer into eight.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. Doubling three times gives two cubed. The common mistake is adding three rather than doubling three times.
lessonContent:
Repeated doubling grows faster than addition.
Model growth processes as multiplication, not sums.
Small exponent differences matter quickly.
Practical folding limits are physical, not mathematical.

title: Squares in Three
question: In a three-by-three grid of small squares, how many squares of every possible size are there in total?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Nine single squares, four two-by-two squares, and one three-by-three square total fourteen.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 14. Counting only the small cells misses the larger squares formed by their combination. Working size by size, from largest to smallest, prevents omissions.
lessonContent:
Composite shapes hide inside simple grids.
Count systematically by size to avoid misses.
Patterns of squares form familiar sequences.
Explicit enumeration beats visual estimation.

title: Squares in Four
question: In a four-by-four grid of small squares, how many squares of all sizes are there altogether?
correctExplanation: Right. Sixteen singles, nine doubles, four triples, and one large square total thirty.

Square counts form a recognisable sequence.

title: Pyramid Corners
question: How many corners does a square-based pyramid have?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The four base corners plus the single apex make five.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. The apex must be counted separately from the base, which is the step people most often forget. Naming each corner one by one prevents the omission.
lessonContent:

Naming each point guards against double counting.

title: Pyramid Edges
question: Counting the line segments where two faces of a square-based pyramid meet, what is the total?
correctExplanation: Right. Four edges around the base plus four slanting edges to the apex total eight.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. The base contributes four and the slanting sides contribute four more. Splitting by type is simpler than trying to trace the outline in one pass.

title: Prism Faces
question: How many faces does a triangular prism have in total?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Two triangular ends plus three rectangular sides make five faces.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Both end triangles count, and the three connecting rectangles complete the total. Forgetting one end is the usual slip.

title: Four-Sided Solid
question: The simplest closed solid is bounded entirely by identical triangles that meet three at each corner. How many triangles enclose it?
correctExplanation: Right. Four triangles enclose the simplest possible solid, with three meeting at each corner.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Its name literally records the count, and each vertex is shared by three faces. The smallest solid in existence has no rectangular sides at all.
lessonContent:

Minimal solids reveal how faces close a volume.
Shared vertices create elegant symmetries.
Simplicity still requires careful counting.

title: Cuts Into Eight
question: What is the minimum number of straight cuts needed to divide a cube into eight equal smaller cubes?
correctExplanation: Exactly. One cut through each of the three axes divides the cube into eight pieces.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Each plane cut splits every existing piece, so three perpendicular planes generate two-by-two-by-two pieces. Cutting each small cube individually would require far more.
lessonContent:
Each cut multiplies the number of pieces.
Planes cut along axes, not individual pieces.
Doubling twice per axis reaches eight in three steps.
Work in dimensions rather than piece by piece.

title: Ant Across Two
question: An ant crawls along a cube's surface from one corner to the diagonally opposite corner by the shortest route. How many faces does the route cross?
correctExplanation: Right. Flattening two adjacent faces into one rectangle makes the shortest path a straight line.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. The trick is to unfold the two faces the ant must use, turning a twisting route into a plain diagonal. Any three-face route is longer because it bends around an extra edge.
lessonContent:
Unfolding converts curved paths into straight ones.
The shortest route often crosses a shared edge.
Flattening is a standard geometric technique.

title: Pentagon Diagonals
question: How many diagonals does a regular pentagon have?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Every corner connects to two non-adjacent corners, and the doubled count halves to five.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Each vertex links to two others that are not neighbours, and dividing by two avoids counting each line twice. The star pattern inside a pentagon traces exactly these lines.
lessonContent:
Diagonals skip neighbours and connect distant vertices.
Counting both directions forces a division by two.
Overcounting then correcting is a standard technique.
Geometry and sequences interconnect repeatedly.

title: Hexagon Diagonals
question: In a regular six-sided figure, how many straight lines join pairs of corners that are not already neighbours?
correctExplanation: Right. Each of six vertices connects to three non-neighbours, and halving the doubled count gives nine.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 9. Progressing from five-sided to six-sided shapes shows the pattern growing by one connection per vertex. Counting per vertex, then halving, is the cleanest path.
lessonContent:
Connection counts grow with the number of vertices.
Per-vertex counting followed by halving avoids errors.
Simple formulas summarise polygon features.
Sequences connect shapes of growing size.

title: Square Symmetry
question: How many lines of symmetry does a non-square rectangle have?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The horizontal and vertical midlines each fold the rectangle onto itself.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. The diagonals do not work because unequal sides fail to overlap, leaving only the two midlines. The square, with equal sides, has four.
lessonContent:

Unequal sides eliminate diagonal folds.
Test each candidate line by folding mentally.
Small property changes alter symmetry deeply.

title: Turned-Over Letter
question: Turning a lowercase letter b through one hundred and eighty degrees produces which lowercase letter?
correctExplanation: Right. The bowl and stem swap sides and directions, turning the b into a q.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is q. A half-turn moves both the stem and the bowl, unlike a mirror flip which would produce a different letter. Tracking both parts of the shape is what makes the rotation reliable.
lessonContent:
Rotation and reflection produce different results.
Track every part of a shape during transformation.
Letters are shapes with orientation properties.
Half-turns reverse both axes at once.
